letters.desc: LPPC's central theme is that state regulators have primary authority over retail rates, generation cost recovery, contract terms, and distribution facilities, and that FERC must expressly disclaim any intent to preempt those state roles.
quotes: LPPC asks that this be accomplished while respecting the role reserved under the Federal Power Act ("FPA") to state authorities over retail service, of which large load is an increasing component.

FERC should clarify that if it proceeds with a NOPR, a proposed rule would be limited to the terms of transmission interconnection. The Commission does not have authority to: (1) establish the terms and conditions of retail service to data centers, including the assessment of up-front generation costs to load and the nature of contractual commitments large load may be asked to make; or (2) mandate transmission service to end use customers (retail wheeling).

LPPC asks the Commission to clarify that the ANOPR's disclaimer reserving authority to states encompasses not only rates for direct retail sales but also the ability of Load Serving Entities ("LSEs") to assess the cost of new generation needed to serve large data centers at the outset of service, and to require contractual commitments of specified length to assure cost recovery.

The Commission should expressly hold that its intention is not to preempt the exercise of state authority over the terms of retail service to large load, including the allocation of generation, distribution upgrade costs, retail contract length, and security requirements.

letters.desc: The filer consistently argues that the MISO region's structure, where states have primary authority over resource adequacy and load interconnection, has produced affordability and reliability advantages. Federal policy should build on this structure rather than bypass it.
quotes: the interconnection of load to the transmission system, regardless of size, is largely a matter of state jurisdiction in MISO and as such, the transmission owner and LSEs play lead and important roles in managing and interconnecting load to the transmission system even before MISO is involved.

any new rules that would attempt to bypass MISO states and MISO members could have the unintended result of making interconnections "more costly, ineffective, and more time consuming," which clearly runs counter to the ANOPR's goals and the goals of this Administration.

letters.org: Office of the Ohio Consumers' Counsel
letters.desc: OCC urges FERC to expressly confirm that states retain authority over retail tariffs and service conditions for large-load customers, citing Ohio's Large Data Center Tariff as an example of state cost-reliability balancing that a federal rule must not displace or duplicate.
quotes: A rule that allows direct transmission interconnections for large end-use customers without coordination with state commissions could undermine local reliability and accountability.
FERC's rule must not undercut or preempt state efforts to manage large-load growth through retail tariffs and rate design.
Ohio's Large Data Center Tariff was developed through state regulatory proceedings to balance the interests of high-load customers with system costs and reliability for existing retail consumers.

The ANOPR makes no mention of the prohibitions in FPA sections 212(g) and (h) on federal regulation of retail marketing areas and of federal regulations "concerning the transmission of electric energy directly to an ultimate consumer."

letters.desc: Sierra Club and its chapter directors argue that federal large load interconnection rules must not undercut state authority to pursue climate and clean energy policies. The concern is that haste to accommodate data centers could override or weaken state-level clean energy goals.
quotes: State efforts to pursue clean energy policies, especially around climate and clean energy, should not be undermined in the rush to power data centers.

Who will pay for the costs imposed across the system by new large loads? How will the connection of these large loads to the grid affect states' abilities to meet their climate and clean energy goals?

letters.desc: SPP raises two state-authority concerns: the SPP Regional State Committee's bylaw-assigned role in cost allocation must be preserved in any final rule, and state laws restricting who may build or own transmission may limit the option-to-build right for load customers.
quotes: SPP requests that any final rule adopted based on this Proposed ANOPR provide the RSC with the opportunity to provide significant input into how network upgrade costs will be allocated within SPP as it relates to the interconnection of large loads.

the Commission should be mindful of state laws that restrict who can build and own transmission. Network Upgrades assigned through SPP's transmission service process can only be assigned to entities that request transmission service.

letters.desc: The GPSC's central argument is that its existing tools under Georgia's vertically integrated structure are adequate to handle large load interconnection, making further FERC rulemaking unnecessary for Georgia. It presents recent tariff changes, the all-source capacity proceeding, and direct stakeholder engagement as proof the state can manage this growth without federal intervention.
quotes: the GPSC has the authority and flexibility to facilitate this growth in a manner that will meet the electricity needs of new customers while protecting existing customers from upward pressure on utility rates.
The GPSC affirms that it is best positioned to ensure the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads with its current policy and regulatory tools.
The vertically integrated market structure in Georgia allows the GPSC to oversee every facet of this load growth and adjust to market conditions as they emerge.

the GPSC has acted in the past year to further solidify its regulatory mandate in response to the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads. In April 2025 the Commission approved changes to its rules and regulations requiring Georgia Power to ensure that new customers over 100 MW pay their cost of service through minimum billing requirements, long term contracts with sizable fees in the case of early termination, and other terms and conditions

The GPSC is also currently conducting an all-source capacity certification proceeding to consider meeting the future needs of Georgia Power customers through cost-effective thermal, renewable, and battery storage technologies.
The GPSC understands that states in other market structures may require different interventions from FERC.
The GPSC will continue to collaborate towards shared goals without the need for further Federal action in Georgia.

letters.desc: Maryland asserts that states have a critical role in demand forecasting, resource planning, and transmission planning integration. The state urges FERC to support rather than hinder state coordination across historically separate planning processes, and to respect NARUC principles preserving state retail regulatory authority.
quotes: states, too, have an important role in ensuring the accuracy of forecast demand

MEA urges FERC to approach transmission-level large load interconnections in a manner that will support and not hinder state decisionmakers as they work to develop and enhance historically siloed state resource, distribution, and transmission planning processes for greater alignment, increased transparency, and more robust stakeholder engagement

FERC actions should not exacerbate affordability and reliability issues, nor constrain state actions on resource decisions, demand response, virtual power plants (VPPs), distributed generation, behind-the-meter generation and energy efficiency
